walkthroughs.body_html:
The Holderness coast (East Yorkshire) loses ~1.8 m/year.

Causes:
• Soft boulder clay cliffs
• Long fetch from North Sea
• Powerful destructive waves

~30 villages lost since Roman times.

In 1991, Mappleton got £2 million defences:

• Two large rock groynes
• Rip-rap at cliff base

But south of Mappleton, erosion sped up — Cowden farm lost land.

Classic winners and losers.

Spurn Point is a 5km sand spit at Holderness's tip.

After 2013 tidal surge cut it in half:
• Council chose managed retreat
• Let nature reshape it
• Saved ongoing maintenance costs

Now part of a nature reserve.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between glacial abrasion and plucking?
options: Abrasion and plucking are different words for the same process.
Abrasion: rock embedded in the glacier base scrapes the bedrock smooth, creating striations. Plucking: meltwater refreezes onto bedrock, then movement rips chunks of rock away.
Abrasion is when wind erodes the glacier and plucking is when rain does.
Lateral moraine is the youngest and terminal moraine is the oldest.

mcqs.q: Why do glaciated valleys have a U-shape rather than a V-shape?
options: Lateral moraine is the youngest and terminal moraine is the oldest.
Glaciers occupy the whole valley width, eroding the sides as well as the floor, producing steep sides and a flat floor (U-shape); rivers erode mainly downwards, leaving V-shape.
Glaciers cut U-shapes because ice is shaped like a U.
Glaciers carve V-shaped valleys just like rivers do.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between lateral, medial and terminal moraine?
options: Moraines are all the same thing — just piles of rocks.
Lateral moraine is the youngest and terminal moraine is the oldest.
Glaciers carve V-shaped valleys just like rivers do.
Lateral moraine forms along the sides of a glacier from rockfall; medial moraine forms where two lateral moraines merge; terminal moraine marks the maximum extent at the snout.
